title: You asked, we answered: The AI boom and gold
gist: The World Gold Council finds the AI boom has not yet visibly increased gold demand (industrial/technology demand was flat at 323t in 2025) because rising AI-chip demand is offset by cost-driven thrifting and miniaturization, but flags co-packaged optics as an emerging AI-data-center technology that could become a new, meaningful source of gold demand, while high-end and safety-critical chips remain effectively gold-irreplaceable.

themes.theme: Gold in electronics: scale and unique properties

insights.claim: Industrial demand for gold in electronics, dentistry and other areas totaled 323 tonnes in 2025, virtually unchanged from 2024, with the electronics sector alone consuming approximately 80% of all gold used in industrial applications.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: The 323t/flat-year-over-year figure is the baseline against which any future AI-driven gold demand shift should be measured, and the 80% electronics concentration means AI-sector chip trends are effectively the single biggest swing factor in industrial gold demand.
insights.quote: In 2025, industrial demand for gold used in electronics, dentistry and other areas totalled 323t, virtually unchanged from 2024.
insights.locator: Gold is used for much more than

insights.claim: Gold's electronics use took off in the 1960s-70s with the rise of semiconductors because it uniquely combines excellent electrical conductivity, corrosion/oxidation resistance, and the ability to be formed into extremely thin wires, films, and coatings without losing performance.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: This combination of properties explains why gold has resisted full substitution for over half a century, a relevant baseline for judging how durable gold's role will remain even as manufacturers push cost-driven thrifting.
insights.quote: Engineers recognised that gold possessed a unique combination of properties that no other material could match: an excellent conductor of electricity and highly resistant to corrosion and oxidation

themes.theme: The AI boom's ambiguous, offsetting effect on gold demand

insights.claim: Despite rapid growth in demand for AI chips, 2025 technology gold demand stayed flat at 323t, because high gold prices push manufacturers to reduce or eliminate gold use and miniaturization means smaller chips need less or no gold, roughly offsetting the demand boost from AI chip growth.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: This directly counters a naive 'AI boom = more gold demand' assumption; investors basing a gold-demand thesis on AI chip growth alone are missing the offsetting cost-thrifting and miniaturization forces that have kept demand flat so far.
insights.quote: We view the current demand situation in the electronics sector very much as a tug-of-war, with cost pressures and technical advances on one side and AI demand on the other. At the moment, the two sides appear evenly matched.
insights.locator: Has the AI boom fuelled demand for gold?

insights.claim: Most 'easy' gold-thrifting (thinning bonding wires and coatings) already happened years ago, meaning most coatings and wires are already at or near their technical minimum thickness, limiting how much further thrifting can reduce gold use per device going forward.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: If thrifting has largely run its course, the offsetting downward force on gold demand may weaken over time, which could tilt the AI-chip-demand versus thrifting 'tug-of-war' toward net demand growth in future years even without new use cases.
insights.quote: “easy” gold-thrifting happened many years ago, meaning that most coatings and wires are already at – or very close to – their technical minimum thickness

themes.theme: Co-packaged optics as an emerging new source of gold demand

insights.claim: Co-packaged optics (CPO), which closely integrates optical communication components with the processor to boost bandwidth and reduce data-transmission bottlenecks for next-generation AI data centers, uses gold in optical/photonic components and high-frequency chip electrodes, and major players including Nvidia are investing heavily in its development despite CPO being at an early adoption stage.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: CPO is flagged as a specific, named emerging technology that could become a new structural source of gold demand if it scales across hyperscale AI infrastructure, giving gold investors a concrete technology trend to monitor for adoption signals (e.g. Nvidia's CPO roadmap) as a demand catalyst.
insights.quote: If the technology achieves widespread deployment across hyperscale AI infrastructure it could represent a small but potentially meaningful new source of demand for gold within the sector.

themes.theme: Gold remains hard to replace in high-end, safety-critical uses

insights.claim: While manufacturers continue to minimize or remove gold in lower-end applications, the World Gold Council believes high-end and safety-critical devices will continue to require gold because manufacturers of complex, costly AI chips prioritize longevity and reliability, which almost always involves gold.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: This suggests gold demand is likely to be resilient specifically in the premium/high-reliability segment of the AI chip market even if commodity electronics keep reducing gold content, a useful demand-durability distinction for gold-market forecasting by product tier.
insights.quote: we believe high-end and safety critical devices will continue to require gold. Many chips and devices used in AI applications are extremely complex and costly; manufacturers seek the best materials to ensure longevity and reliability

themes.theme: Gold's other indispensable, if small, industrial roles

insights.claim: Beyond electronics, gold is used in aerospace, chemical catalysis, optical applications, and healthcare diagnostics, where billions of diagnostic tests annually rely on tiny gold particles to provide rapid, accurate diagnosis of diseases like malaria, sepsis, and HIV/AIDS, including in locations with limited infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Louise Street and Trevor Keel
insights.so_what: Even though these niche applications don't move aggregate gold demand meaningfully, the diagnostic-test use case shows a distinct, non-AI-linked structural demand floor tied to global healthcare infrastructure that persists independent of the AI/electronics cycle.
insights.quote: billions of diagnostic tests are manufactured on an annual basis, the vast majority of which rely on tiny particles of gold to provide rapid and accurate diagnosis of diseases like malaria, sepsis and HIV/AIDs
